code.title: 500 tasks without 500 threads

followUps: Create a dedicated Thread for work that runs for the whole life of the process or must not share the pool: a long-running background loop, a thread that needs a specific priority, apartment state (STA for COM/UI) or a stable name, or code that blocks for a long time. A blocked pool thread starves other work, while your own thread only costs its ~1 MB stack. Example: one consumer loop that blocks on a queue for hours. new Thread(Loop){IsBackground=true}.Start(); or Task.Factory.StartNew(..., TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning).

code.title: Hand-written async state machine

followUps: It means the ambient state of the caller (such as AsyncLocal values, culture, security principal) is captured when you await and restored when the continuation runs, so the code after the await sees the same values as before it. Example: an AsyncLocal<string> holding a request id is still "req-7" after await Task.Delay(10), even on another thread. The cost is a small capture per await; ExecutionContext.SuppressFlow() turns it off for work that does not need it.

Because the method is not actually asynchronous: the compiler still builds a state machine, but with no await it runs fully synchronously and returns a completed task, so you pay the overhead for nothing. It also usually means the author expected it to run in the background, which it will not. Warning CS1998 hints at this. Fix by removing async and returning Task.FromResult(x) or Task.CompletedTask, or by adding the real await.

code.title: Sync-over-async deadlock on a single-thread context

followUps: It is when every thread-pool thread is stuck waiting, so the queued work that could free them never gets a thread. Example: with a minimum of 8 threads, 8 requests each call .Result on a task whose continuation is queued to the pool. All 8 threads wait, the continuations wait in the queue, and the pool adds only about 1 or 2 new threads per second, so latency grows while CPU stays near 0 percent. The cure is to stop blocking and use await.

code.title: Counting context hops with ConfigureAwait(false)

followUps: No. It only says the continuation does not need the captured context. If the awaited task is already complete, the code continues synchronously on the same thread with no switch at all. If it is not complete, the continuation runs wherever the task finishes, or on the thread pool, which may or may not be a different thread than before. Example: await Task.FromResult(1).ConfigureAwait(false) never changes thread. Do not rely on a specific thread either way.

code.title: WhenAll keeps every exception, WhenAny returns the task

followUps:
Wrap the tasks so the first failure cancels the others and is thrown at once. Steps: 1) share a CancellationTokenSource; 2) wrap each task in a helper that cancels it when it faults; 3) await WhenAny repeatedly, or await the first faulted task. Short version:

var pending = new List<Task>(tasks);
while (pending.Count > 0) {
  Task t = await Task.WhenAny(pending);
  await t;            // rethrows at the first failure
  pending.Remove(t);
}

This is O(N^2) in removals but fine for small N; the losers still need cancelling.

code.title: Cooperative cancellation and linked tokens

followUps: Check which token fired. Pass the caller token and a timeout token through a linked source, then in the catch compare: catch (OperationCanceledException) when (callerToken.IsCancellationRequested) means the caller cancelled; if it is false but your timeout source IsCancellationRequested, it was your timeout, so you can throw a TimeoutException. Example: a 2 s timeout with the caller token never cancelled gives timeout. Without this check both look identical.

code.title: ValueTask: synchronous hit, async miss

followUps: Because the pooled source is reused: once you await the ValueTask, the source is reset and handed to the next operation. A second await then reads state that now belongs to someone else, so you can get a wrong result, an exception, or a corrupted state with no warning. Example: await it once, the object is recycled for call B, and your second await returns B's value. A Task has no such issue because it is never reused. Call AsTask() once if you need to await several times.

code.title: Pull-based async stream with early exit

followUps: Pass the token to the iterator method with the [EnumeratorCancellation] attribute and call WithCancellation(token) on the consumer: await foreach (var x in GetPages().WithCancellation(ct)). The token is then delivered to the parameter, so inside the iterator you pass it to awaits and call ThrowIfCancellationRequested. Without the attribute the token you passed to the method and the one passed via WithCancellation stay separate. Breaking out of the loop also disposes the iterator, which runs its finally blocks.

code.title: Limiting concurrency with SemaphoreSlim

followUps:
Give each operation its own timeout using a linked token: create a source per call with CancelAfter, so a slow call fails alone instead of holding a slot forever. Example: limit 5, 2 s each:

await gate.WaitAsync(ct);
try {
  using var cts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(ct);
  cts.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));
  await CallAsync(item, cts.Token);
} finally { gate.Release(); }

Start the timer after getting the slot, otherwise queue time counts against it.

code.title: TaskCompletionSource continuations inside a lock

followUps:
Make a TaskCompletionSource with RunContinuationsAsynchronously and expose a Wait task and a Set method; Reset swaps in a fresh source. Steps: 1) keep a field tcs; 2) WaitAsync returns tcs.Task; 3) Set calls tcs.TrySetResult(true); 4) Reset replaces tcs only if it is already completed.

class AsyncEvent {
  volatile TaskCompletionSource<bool> tcs = New();
  static TaskCompletionSource<bool> New() => new(TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously);
  public Task WaitAsync() => tcs.Task;
  public void Set() => tcs.TrySetResult(true);
  public void Reset() { if (tcs.Task.IsCompleted) tcs = New(); }
}

code.title: Thread-pool starvation with a 2-thread pool

followUps: Because the code inside is already running on a pool thread and the ASP.NET Core request has no context to escape, so Task.Run just adds a hop and an extra queue item. It does not free the request from waiting, and if the work is I/O the thread is simply blocked on another pool thread, so you use two threads instead of one. Example: await Task.Run(() => client.GetAsync(url)) only adds overhead; call the async API directly. Task.Run helps only to move heavy CPU work off a UI thread.

code.title: Predicting A, B, C ordering

followUps: Task.Yield forces the method to return to its caller at once and continue later, as if the await was incomplete. The output is still A, B, C, but now by design rather than because of a timer: "A" prints, F returns an incomplete task, the caller prints "B", and the continuation (queued to the context or pool) prints "C". Without Yield and with no real await, the order would be A, C, B. Yield is a way to release a thread in a long loop or force asynchrony.

code.title: Eager vs lazy argument validation

followUps: Yes, with a twist: an async iterator (async IAsyncEnumerable<T> with yield return) does not even run any code until the first MoveNextAsync, so argument checks inside are delayed even more, until the first item is requested. The fix is the same: a normal public method checks arguments and returns the private iterator. Example: public IAsyncEnumerable<int> Read(string p) { if (p == null) throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(p)); return Core(p); }. The call then throws at once, not when the loop begins.

code.title: Task.Run unwraps, StartNew does not

followUps: Use LongRunning when the work will occupy a thread for a long time, for example a loop that runs for the life of the app or blocks on a queue. It tells the scheduler to start a dedicated thread instead of tying up a pool thread, which would otherwise delay other work and trigger slow thread injection. Example: Task.Factory.StartNew(Loop, TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning) for a consumer that blocks for hours. For short CPU work or any async work, do not use it; plain Task.Run is right.
